prompt: Write a personal essay about moving to a new city. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
The moving truck pulled away at four in the afternoon on a Tuesday, and I stood on the sidewalk in front of a building I had never seen before, in a city I had visited exactly once, holding a set of keys that didn't yet feel like mine. The driver had waved cheerfully as he drove off, as if he were delivering me to something wonderful, and maybe he was, but in that moment all I could feel was the strange vertigo of being utterly unanchored.

I had lived in the same town for twenty-six years. Not the same house, but the same streets, the same grocery store where the cashiers knew my face, the same park where I'd learned to ride a bike and later, awkwardly, to kiss someone. My whole sense of the world was built on that accumulated familiarity, the kind you don't notice until it's gone. I thought I understood what I was giving up when I accepted the job in the new city. I made lists. I researched neighborhoods. I told myself, and everyone who asked, that this was the right move, the brave move, the move that people make when they're building a life.

Nobody tells you that homesickness is physical. I expected it to be emotional, and it was, but there were whole weeks when my body simply felt wrong, the way it does when you're sleeping in a bed that isn't yours. I woke up disoriented. I got lost going to the post office, a fifteen-minute walk from my apartment. I stood in the cereal aisle of a supermarket and felt close to tears because I couldn't find the brand I'd eaten since childhood, which is absurd, and I knew it was absurd even as it was happening. Grief, I learned, does not only come from death. It comes from dislocation, from the sudden subtraction of everything your days were made of.

For the first two months, I lived like a tourist who had rented an apartment by mistake. I worked, I came home, I ate pasta standing at the counter, and on weekends I called my mother and my old friends and slowly reassembled my old life over the phone. The new city remained a backdrop, a set of unfamiliar streets I moved through without touching. I remember thinking, with some despair, that I might simply live like this forever: physically present, emotionally elsewhere, a person occupying a city without belonging to it.

The change, when it came, came by accident. It was a Sunday in October, rain coming down in the sideways way this city does rain, and the café where I'd been hiding with a book closed early. The barista, a woman named Ruth who I'd exchanged maybe ten words with, told me about a dumpling place two blocks away that never closed early. I went. The owner gave me the wrong order and then, apologizing, the right one for free. And then, because it was raining and the place was nearly empty and I had nowhere to be, I stayed. I watched the family who ran it eat their own dinner at a corner table. A little girl did her homework beside the register. Somebody's grandmother criticized everybody's posture.

It was nothing. It was everything. I walked home soaked and strangely elated, and I remember thinking: I know a place now. One place. It was the first stone in what I hoped would eventually be a bridge.

After that, I set about the slow, deliberate work of collecting places. A laundromat. A bench by the river where the light came good at six in the evening. A bookstore with a dog that slept in the window. None of this happened quickly, and none of it happened naturally. I am a shy person, and the friendships that eventually formed took months of small talk and mutual risk, of saying yes to invitations I wanted to decline. But I discovered something that I think is true for most people and that nobody had told me: belonging is not something that happens to you. It is a series of small, repeated acts of choosing to stay, of choosing to notice, of choosing to walk into the room even when you'd rather be home.

It has been almost three years now. Last week, a new coworker asked me for restaurant recommendations and I heard myself reeling off twelve, with opinions, with lore, with warnings about which ones had gone downhill. Afterward I realized that I had sounded like a person who lived here. Because I was. Somewhere between that first dumpling place and now, between the lost weekends and the river bench, the city stopped being "the city" and became, simply, here.

I don't want to romanticize it. I still miss my hometown; I probably always will. When I go back to visit, I feel a pull that this city has never quite matched, a tenderness toward streets that know my whole history. But I've made a kind of peace with carrying both places inside me. Home, I've come to think, is not a single address. It is whatever you've had the patience to grow. And growth, as any gardener will tell you, begins with a hole in the ground and a period of looking very much like nothing is happening.

I stood on that sidewalk three years ago feeling unanchored. I understand now that I wasn't unanchored; I was just between anchors. The new one took time to set. But it set. Somewhere out there, someone is standing on their own unfamiliar sidewalk with their own unfamiliar keys, certain that they've made a terrible mistake. I want to tell them what nobody told me: give it a year. Give it two. Learn the name of one barista. Find the bench where the light comes right. You are not lost. You are just early.
